chapters.title: Chapter 6: Using Financial Statements at Work

lessons.title: Red Flags in Financial Statements Every Manager Should Recognise

children.text: You are not an auditor and you will never be asked to detect a fraud. What you will be asked to do is decide whether to sign a three-year contract with a supplier, extend ₹4 crore of credit to a new distributor, accept a job offer from a company you have never analysed, or support an acquisition your CEO is excited about.
For all four, the skill is the same: noticing when the numbers stop making sense together. Most warning signs are visible in published statements long before anything becomes news.

body.text: Frauds are rare. Deterioration is common. Both announce themselves the same way, through numbers that no longer agree with each other.

children.text: The Eight Signals Worth Knowing

body.caption: What to look for, and where

cells: Profit without cash
Operating cash far below profit for several years
Sales are being recorded but not collected, or profit is soft
Cash flow statement, compared with the P&L
Working capital drift
Receivables or inventory growing much faster than revenue
Channel stuffing, ageing stock, or customers in trouble
Balance sheet across three years, and the ageing note
Other income propping up profit
A large share of profit before tax coming from outside the core business
Operations are weaker than the headline suggests
Other income line and its note
Aggressive capitalisation
Capital work in progress rising for years, or costs capitalised that peers expense
Expenses parked on the balance sheet to protect reported profit
Property, plant and equipment note, and accounting policies
Convenient estimate changes
Useful lives extended, provisioning rates cut, revenue recognition policy changed
Profit managed by assumption rather than by performance
Accounting policies note and the change in estimates disclosure
Related party build-up
Growing sales, purchases, loans or guarantees involving group entities
Value moving between entities, or circular revenue
Related party transactions note
Funding stress
Short-term borrowings rising, long-term assets funded by working capital lines, high promoter pledging
Refinancing risk that a profitable P&L can hide
Borrowings note, and shareholding disclosures on NSE or BSE
Governance churn
Auditor resigns mid-term, CFO leaves abruptly, results are delayed, opinion is qualified
The people closest to the numbers are uncomfortable
Auditor's report, exchange announcements, board changes

body.text: No single signal proves anything. A company can capitalise heavily because it is genuinely building a plant, and a CFO can leave for an excellent job. What matters is clustering. Three or four signals appearing together, in the same direction, over two or three years, is the pattern worth acting on.

body.title: Run the cash test
body.prompt: A company reports profit after tax of ₹40 crore and cash from operations of ₹12 crore for the year. What is the ratio of operating cash to profit?
body.explanation: ₹12 crore ÷ ₹40 crore = 0.30. One such year can be explained by growth or a one-off. Three consecutive years near this level means the reported profits are not being converted into money, which is the most reliable single warning in financial statements.

children.text: How Deterioration Actually Unfolds
Trouble rarely arrives suddenly. In the published numbers it usually runs to a recognisable schedule.

events.title: Receivables start stretching
events.description: Revenue grows nicely. Receivable days move from 60 to 75. Nobody comments, because profit is up and the growth story is intact.

events.title: Cash and profit separate
events.description: Operating cash falls well below profit. Short-term borrowings rise to fund the gap. Other income starts appearing more prominently in the profit build.

events.title: Accounting gets creative
events.description: Useful lives are extended, a provisioning policy is relaxed, or costs are capitalised. Related party loans and advances grow. Results are filed close to the deadline.

events.title: The people leave
events.description: The auditor resigns or issues a qualified opinion, the CFO departs, a rating is downgraded, and a repayment is missed. Only now does it become news.

children.text: Two well-documented Indian cases bracket the range. In January 2009, the chairman of Satyam Computer Services admitted in a letter to the board that the company's accounts had been falsified over years, including cash and bank balances that did not exist. In 2018, the IL&FS group defaulted on debt repayments despite reporting profits, having funded long-term infrastructure assets with shorter-term borrowing. One was fabrication and one was structural, and in both the published statements carried signals for years.

body.title: Which combination worries you most?
body.question: Which set of facts is the strongest reason to slow down before signing a three-year supply contract?
options: Profit fell 20% this year after a plant fire, with insurance recovery pending
Revenue up 18%, receivable days up from 62 to 96, operating cash negative for the third year, and a new auditor appointed after the previous one resigned
The company took a large term loan to build a new plant, raising debt to equity from 0.4 to 0.9
Other income rose because the company earned more interest on its cash surplus
body.explanation: The second option clusters four signals pointing the same way: growth that is not being collected, three years of cash drain, and an auditor who walked away. The others each have an ordinary explanation visible in the same statements.

children.text: Aggressive Is Not the Same as Illegal
Most of what a manager will encounter is not fraud. It is choices made within the rules, pushed to the edge. Both companies below comply with Ind AS.

columns.label: Conservative choices
points: Recognises revenue on delivery and acceptance
Discloses contingent liabilities fully and plainly

columns.label: Aggressive choices
points: Extends laptop life to five years, lowering the annual charge
Provides only for receivables over 365 days
Capitalises implementation costs as an intangible
Recognises revenue on dispatch, before acceptance
Describes contingent liabilities vaguely and briefly

children.text: The aggressive company reports higher profit every year without selling anything more. Nothing here is illegal, and the difference shows up only in the accounting policies note, which is why that note deserves five minutes when you are comparing two companies.

body.text: Watch for changes, not just levels. A company that has always depreciated over five years is being consistent. A company that changes to five years in a weak quarter, and discloses it in a single line, is managing its profit. The disclosure of a change in accounting estimate is mandatory, so the information is there. It is simply small.

body.title: Where each red flag is disclosed

children.text: Everything in this lesson is published. Knowing which note holds what turns a vague suspicion into a specific question.
Related party transactions note:

every sale, purchase, loan, guarantee and remuneration involving group entities, directors and their relatives. Under SEBI's listing regulations, related party transactions above a materiality threshold linked to consolidated turnover need shareholder approval, and the threshold has been revised over time.
Contingent liabilities and commitments note:
disputed tax demands, guarantees given for other group companies, pending litigation. These do not appear in the balance sheet totals and can be very large.
Auditor's report:
the opinion paragraph, any qualification, emphasis of matter, going concern paragraph, and key audit matters. The CARO annexure adds specifics on defaults, loans and statutory dues.
Accounting policies and estimates:
useful lives, provisioning norms, revenue recognition, and any change made during the year.
Shareholding and exchange filings:
promoter pledging, auditor resignation letters, board changes and results delays are all filed with NSE and BSE.

body.label: NFRA: National Financial Reporting Authority
body.description: India's audit regulator publishes inspection reports and orders against audit firms. Useful context when you want to know how rigorous the audit environment around a company has been.

body.title: The paragraph nobody wants
body.textWithBlank: When an auditor doubts a company's ability to continue operating, the audit report includes a material uncertainty related to ___ concern.
body.explanation: A going concern paragraph is the most serious routine signal in an audit report. It means the auditor is not confident the company can meet its obligations over the next year without something changing.

body.title: The distributor who wants ₹4 crore of credit
body.scenario: You head sales for the eastern region at Kesari Foods. A new distributor in Guwahati wants ₹4 crore of credit and a 90-day cycle, promising ₹25 crore of annual volume. They are a private limited company, so there is no annual report on any website. Your target is short by ₹6 crore and the quarter ends in five weeks.
body.prompt: How would you check them, and what would you propose?
body.modelAnswer:
What to check, cheaply and fast:
1. MCA master data for the company: incorporation date, paid-up capital, directors, and whether annual filings are up to date. A company that has not filed for two years is an immediate no.
2. Buy their last two filed financial statements from the MCA portal. Look at net worth, borrowings, receivable and payable days, and whether operating cash is positive.
3. Check charges registered on their assets, which shows how much is already pledged to lenders, and check for any related party lending out of the company.
4. Ask for bank references and the last six months of bank statements for the main account, plus GST filing status, which shows whether declared turnover is real and current.
5. Trade references from two existing principals, asked specifically about payment behaviour, not about the relationship.
What the numbers must clear:
6. ₹4 crore of credit against ₹25 crore of annual volume is about 58 days of sales, before the 90-day cycle is even honoured. If their net worth is smaller than the credit I am extending, I am funding their business, not selling to them.
What I would propose:
7. Start at ₹1 crore of credit and 45 days for two quarters, with the limit rising on demonstrated payment behaviour.
8. Security proportionate to the risk: a bank guarantee, post-dated instruments, or a personal guarantee from the promoters.
9. Credit insurance if the company uses it, which prices the risk independently of my target.
10. Escalate the quarter-end pressure honestly to my leadership. A ₹6 crore gap filled by a ₹4 crore uncollectable receivable is not a gap filled, and Lesson 1.1 showed exactly how that arithmetic ends.

body.title: The ten-minute scan
steps: Compare operating cash with profit after tax for the last three years.
Compare growth in receivables and inventory with growth in revenue over the same period.
Check how much of profit before tax came from other income.
Read the auditor's opinion paragraph and the key audit matters.
Read the related party transactions note and the contingent liabilities note.
Check short-term borrowings against long-term assets, and look for any auditor or CFO change in the last two years.

cards.definition: The assumption that a company can continue operating. A material uncertainty here is a serious audit signal.
An audit opinion stating that the accounts are fine except for specified issues.
A paragraph drawing attention to something significant without qualifying the opinion.
A transaction with group entities, directors or their relatives, disclosed in a dedicated note.
A possible obligation, such as a disputed tax demand or a guarantee, disclosed in the notes but not in the balance sheet totals.
Pushing stock onto distributors to record revenue that will not be cleanly collected.
Promoters borrowing against their shareholding, disclosed in exchange filings and a sign of funding stress.
Using accounting choices and estimates, within the rules, to shape reported profit.

points: Managers need to spot deterioration, not fraud, and the published statements usually show it first.
The most reliable single test is operating cash against profit, read over three years rather than one.
Watch for clusters. Three or four signals moving the same way matter far more than any one of them alone.
Aggressive accounting is legal and common. It lives in the accounting policies note and in changes to estimates.
The notes carry what the face of the statements does not: related party dealings, contingent liabilities and guarantees.
When a company is unlisted, MCA filings, GST status, bank references and registered charges do the same job.

body.text: Kesari Foods and the Guwahati distributor are fictional. The references to Satyam Computer Services in 2009 and the IL&FS group in 2018 describe widely reported events and are used only as teaching examples. Nothing here is investment advice or an assessment of any current company.
